summary:
Sweden's parliament approved new acts on legal gender recognition and on medical procedures performed on genitalia in April 2024, as recorded by a Library of Congress global legal monitor entry of April 2024.

The Legal Gender Recognition Act came into force on 1 July 2025. TGEU reports that the new act simplifies the procedure for changing legal gender but falls short of a full self-determination model, with medical barriers remaining, so a person seeking to update legal documents may still be required to satisfy medical conditions.

Sweden's main national board decided on 28 January 2017 that transgender people would no longer be classified as mentally ill, the depathologisation step that governs diagnostic status for trans residents.

The clearest documented everyday-facility friction concerns changing rooms. SVT reported in October 2025 that the swimming-pool chain Medley stopped trans customers from choosing their changing rooms, a restriction on facility access that a trans visitor to such a venue would encounter directly.

On hate crime, Brå (the National Council for Crime Prevention) published report 2024:13, which supplements Swedish hate-crime statistics with a descriptive analysis of persons suspected of offences in which police identified LGBTQI-related hate-crime motives. This is the national dataset on anti-LGBTQI offending.

On protection machinery, the ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2026 covering 2025 records a bill that would extend protection of victims of conversion practices when these are carried out through coercion, threats or sustained psychological pressure.
tangentialFactors:
The 2019 edition of the Spartacus Gay Travel Index, reported by Newsweek, placed Canada, Portugal and Sweden in a tie as the most LGBT-friendly travel destinations, third-party evidence on Sweden's standing as a visitor destination and a point of comparison against the facility-access restriction reported by SVT.

An open-access article in Sexuality Research and Social Policy (4 February 2016, volume 13, pages 119 to 129) traces LGBT policy development in Sweden's military from 1944 to 2014, the historical record behind current service conditions rather than a statement of them.

In November 2025 the Church of Sweden decided that new priests must be willing to marry same-sex couples, passing with 141 votes at the 2025 Church Council. This is an LGB-facing measure and does not itself address trans status.
localsOnly:
The depathologisation decision of 28 January 2017 removed the classification of transgender people as mentally ill from Sweden's main national board, changing the diagnostic status recorded for trans residents rather than the position of visitors.

The Legal Gender Recognition Act in force from 1 July 2025 governs how residents change legal gender; TGEU's assessment is that medical barriers remain for them despite the simplified procedure.

The conversion-practices bill recorded in the ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2026 would protect residents subjected to coercion, threats or sustained psychological pressure, and the Church of Sweden's November 2025 requirement binds its own clergy.

Brå report 2024:13 is a resident-facing statistical study of persons suspected of offences with identified LGBTQI-related hate-crime motives, produced for the national crime-prevention record.
outOfScopeNotes:
The source inventory contains nothing on criminalisation, on the law governing bathroom access, or on visa, entry and border-screening procedures, so those points are unresolved here rather than assessed.

The scope of the Medley changing-room restriction is not stated: whether it applies across all of the chain's venues, whether it has been challenged in court, and whether comparable policies exist at other Swedish swimming facilities are unresolved on these sources.

Brå report 2024:13 is described in the inventory only by subject; the number of hate-crime reports, the number of suspects and any conviction outcomes are not sourced here.

The conversion-practices measure is recorded as a bill, and whether it was enacted is not stated in the inventory.

The military article ends at 2014, so current service conditions for trans personnel in the Swedish armed forces are not sourced.

The Spartacus Gay Travel Index reference dates from 2019 and is a third-party ranking, not an official assessment.
